# Adjudication Task — Chapter 619

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃619화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|독화루(毒華樓)라…….
  6|
  7|온갖 독물이 득실거리는 남만에 잘 어울리는 이름이다. 다만 객잔이나 기루보다는 와르르 맨션에 가깝다는 점이 함정이지만.
  8|
  9|‘천면호리가 알려 준 대로라면 여기가 맞긴 할 텐데.’
 10|
 11|미심쩍은 눈빛으로 낡아 부스러지기 직전의 목제 건물을 바라보던 그때, 이방인들을 둘러싼 주위의 분위기는 시시각각 흉흉해지고 있었다.
 12|
 13|“빌어먹을 한족 놈들!”
 14|
 15|“네놈들 땅으로 돌아가라!”
 16|
 17|쉬익! 딱!
 18|
 19|뒤통수로 날아드는 짱돌을 피해 낸 사마표가 한숨처럼 중얼거렸다.
 20|
 21|“각주, 그냥 들어가는 게 낫겠는데. 당장 저들과 싸울 게 아니라면.”
 22|
 23|“그건 곤란하지.”
 24|
 25|적어도 이번만큼은 녀석의 말이 백번 옳았다.
 26|
 27|남만에 도착하자마자 토착민 전체를 적으로 돌릴 수는 없으니까.
 28|
 29|나는 살벌한 기세를 뿜어내는 이민족 무리를 힐끗 바라본 뒤 독화루의 문을 열었다.
 30|
 31|끼이이익.
 32|
 33|낡아빠진 목제 문이 힘없는 마찰음을 토해 낸다.
 34|
 35|흐릿한 불빛과 음울한 분위기에 잠긴 객잔 내부. 잡초처럼 듬성듬성 자리 잡은 조잡한 탁자를 사이에 두고 앉아 있던 선객들이 이쪽을 향해 고개를 돌렸다.
 36|
 37|“못 보던 얼굴인…… 한족?”
 38|
 39|“카악, 퉤.”
 40|
 41|히드라인가.
 42|
 43|이 동네 사람들은 가래를 아주 패시브 스킬처럼 쓰는구만.
 44|
 45|먼지 쌓인 바닥에 침을 탁 뱉은 이민족 손님들은 불콰하게 달아오른 얼굴로 자리에서 일어났다.
 46|
 47|“여기가 어디라고 감히 한족 놈들이. 죽고 싶어서 환장을 한 건가?”
 48|
 49|“술맛도 떨어졌으니 이만 나가세. 저놈들이랑 함께 있어 봤자 좋을 게 없어.”
 50|
 51|쾅!
 52|
 53|큰소리와 함께 문이 닫히자 주화란이 복잡한 표정으로 입을 열었다.
 54|
 55|“뭔가 단단히 틀어진 모양이에요. 지난번에 왔을 때만 해도 분명 이 정도는 아니었는데.”
 56|
 57|송일섬도 고개를 끄덕이며 동조했다.
 58|
 59|“내 생각도 같다. 남만의 이민족들이 경계심이 심한 건 사실이지만, 적어도 중원과 가장 가깝게 맞닿아 있는 영인(永仁)만큼은 달랐어.”
 60|
 61|“맞아요. 그래서 비록 흔한 일은 아니었지만, 중원의 상단이나 표국이 오가던 곳이기도 했고요. 그런데 왜…….”
 62|
 63|주화란이 말꼬리를 흐리던 그때. 어디선가 늙수그레한 목소리가 불쑥 끼어들었다.
 64|
 65|“왜긴. 바로 그 표국 때문이지. 자네들과 같은 한족 놈들 말이야.”
 66|
 67|독화루에 남아 있던 사람은 우리뿐만이 아니었다.
 68|
 69|조금 전까지만 하더라도 술에 떡이 된 채 자고 있던 노인은, 굽은 허리를 두드리며 말을 이었다.
 70|
 71|“재수 옴 붙은 게지. 이런 상황에 멋모르고 남만까지 기어들어 온 자네들도. 그런 겁 없는 한족 놈들 때문에 장사 공치게 생긴 어떤 늙은이도.”
 72|
 73|노인의 정체를 알아차린 내가 물었다.
 74|
 75|“여기 주인장 되십니까?”
 76|
 77|입술 사이로 흘러나오는 유창한 이민족의 언어에, 노인이 뜻밖이라는 눈빛으로 나를 바라보았다.
 78|
 79|“이곳 말을 할 줄 아는군. 혹시 묘족(苗族) 출신인가?”
 80|
 81|“아뇨.”
 82|
 83|“그렇다고 백족이나 만족 같지는 않고. 상판을 보아하니 한족이 틀림없는데…… 말이 놀라울 만큼 능숙하군. 여기서 나고 자란 사람이라고 해도 믿을 정도야.”
 84|
 85|역시 [통합언어팩]. 성능 하나는 확실하지.
 86|
 87|내 유창한 발음에 주화란도 놀란 표정을 지을 정도다.
 88|
 89|“이민족들의 언어는 언제 익히셨어요?”
 90|
 91|“음, 그거야 뭐.”
 92|
 93|미주알고주알 설명할 수도 없는 문제라, 말꼬리를 흐린 나는 천연덕스럽게 대답했다.
 94|
 95|“그냥 어쩌다가 보니 익히게 된 잡기예요.”
 96|
 97|옆자리에 앉은 혁무진이 작은 목소리로 중얼거렸다.
 98|
 99|“조장님이 할 줄 아는 건 주색잡기밖에 없었는데…….”
100|
101|“시벌놈이.”
102|
103|빡!
104|
105|“어억!”
106|
107|명치를 붙잡고 쓰러지는 혁무진의 모습에 노인이 혀를 찼다.
108|
109|“맞을 말만 골라서 하는 놈이로군.”
110|
111|“원래 저런 놈이니까 신경 쓰지 마시고…… 잠깐. 한어를 할 줄 아십니까?”
112|
113|“어느 정도는. 젊었을 적에는 한족들과의 통역도 여러 번 맡았었지.”
114|
115|대수롭지 않다는 듯이 대답한 노인이 뼈마디밖에 남지 않은 손가락으로 송일섬을 가리켰다.
116|
117|“저 컴컴하게 생긴 자는 제법 익숙한 얼굴인데, 혹시 삼 년 전쯤 이곳에 온 적이 있지 않나?”
118|
119|따지고 보면 가장 눈에 띄는 것은 주화란이었을 텐데, 인피면구를 착용해서인지 송일섬을 가장 먼저 알아본다.
120|
121|송일섬이 묵묵히 고개를 끄덕이자, 노인이 무릎을 탁 쳤다.
122|
123|“그럴 줄 알았지. 거기 이름이 아마 용왕…….”
124|
125|“용봉표국이오. 용왕이 아니라.”
126|
127|“그래. 용봉표국. 중원의 다른 상단이나 표국과는 달리 일 년에 두어 번씩 오던 한족들이라 똑똑히 기억하고 있지.”
128|
129|똑똑히 기억한 것치고는 이름부터 틀렸는데요.
130|
131|근질거리는 입을 참은 나는, 아까부터 노인에게 묻고 싶었던 질문을 던졌다.
132|
133|“그런데 조금 전에 하신 말씀은 뭡니까?”
134|
135|“응? 뭐가?”
136|
137|“표국 때문에 이렇게 됐다고 하셨잖습니까. 하신 말씀을 그대로 옮기자면, 우리 같은 한족 놈들 때문에요.”
138|
139|노인이 뚱한 표정으로 되물었다.
140|
141|“내가? 언제?”
142|
143|“예? 분명히 그러셨…….”
144|
145|“도통 기억이 안 나는데.”
146|
147|기억이 안 나긴 개뿔이. 노인의 태도에서 뭔가를 깨달은 내가 한숨처럼 입을 열었다.
148|
149|“식사. 지금 바로 준비됩니까?”
150|
151|“아, 당연히 되지. 돈만 주면 뭐든 해 줄 테니 걱정 말라고.”
152|
153|식사라는 두 글자에, 죽어 가는 표정으로 탁자에 엎드려 있던 태산이 벌떡 일어나며 부르짖었다.
154|
155|“태산이! 오향장육 먹고 싶다!”
156|
157|“무식할 만큼 기운찬 놈이 하나 있었군. 그럼 닭고기를 준비해 주지.”
158|
159|“왜째서 닭고기! 태산이 싫다! 오향장육!”
160|
161|오향장육을 해 달라는데 왜 닭고기로 변경되었는지는 모르겠지만, 지금은 최대한 노인의 비위를 맞춰야 한다.
162|
163|나는 곧장 지랄 발광을 떨어 대는 태산을 막을 한 사람의 이름을 불렀다.
164|
165|“마표야. 뭐하냐.”
166|
167|“사마표다.”
168|
169|“그래, 사표야.”
170|
171|“……태산. 그만하고 자리에 앉아라.”
172|
173|기분 나쁜 표정으로 나를 노려본 사마표가 태산을 진정시키는 사이, 노인은 천연덕스럽게 손을 내밀고 있었다.
174|
175|“뭡니까?”
176|
177|“선결제일세.”
178|
179|“아.”
180|
181|“어디 보자. 일인일계(一人一鷄)는 기본이니 닭 다섯 마리가 필요하겠군. 게다가 마리 당 은자 한 냥으로 쳐서…… 도합 은자 열 냥일세.”
182|
183|“……은자 열 냥이요? 심지어 마리당 한 냥이면 은자 다섯 냥인데?”
184|
185|“그런가? 그럼 마리 당 두 냥으로 하세나.”
186|
187|“예?”
188|
189|노인이 당당하게 대답했다.
190|
191|“아. 마리당 두 냥으로 하자고.”
192|
193|“…….”
194|
195|“싫으면 침 뱉고 나가든가. 참고로 인근 백 리 안에 다른 마을은 없네.”
196|
197|미친 배짱 장사 보소. 한 오십 년 전쯤 용산에서 태어났다면 건물주가 되었을 양반이다.
198|
199|‘웬일로 오는 길에 산적을 안 만나나 했는데, 산이 아니라 객잔에 있었네.’
200|
201|날강도나 다름없는 가격이었지만 지금은 돈 아낄 때가 아니다.
202|
203|나는 무림맹에서 활동비로 받아 온 두둑한 전낭에서 은자 열 개를 꺼내어 노인에게 건넸다.
204|
205|“자. 은자 열 냥입니다.”
206|
207|“한족치고는 제법 말귀가 통하는군.”
208|
209|촤르륵.
210|
211|번쩍이는 은자를 쓸어 담은 노인이 씩 웃었다.
212|
213|“그건 그렇고. 술은?”
214|
215|“술은 괜찮습니다.”
216|
217|“마셔.”
218|
219|“…….”
220|
221|“마시라고.”
222|
223|이제는 뭐라 대꾸할 기력도 없다.
224|
225|나는 침울한 표정으로 다시 전낭을 열었다.
226|
227|
228|
229|* * *
230|
231|
232|
233|남만에서의 첫 식사는 다른 의미로 대단했다.
234|
235|영양실조에 걸려 비쩍 마른 닭 요리. 그리고 누군가 먹다 남긴 것이 분명해 보이는 키핑 화주(火酒).
236|
237|이딴 걸로 은자 수십 냥씩이나 받아먹는 것도 놀라웠지만, 그중 상당수가 노인의 입에 들어갔다는 사실만큼은 아니었다.
238|
239|“꺼윽. 잘 먹었다.”
240|
241|“…….”
242|
243|아니, 왜 우리가 아니라 당신이 잘 먹은 건데.
244|
245|그런 의문이 목구멍 끝까지 차올랐지만 간신히 참았다. 돈과 식사를 바치는 대가로 정보를 얻었으니까.
246|
247|“천마표국이요?”
248|
249|“그래. 기억하기로는 분명 사천(四川)에서 왔다고 했어. 여인 하나에 다른 사내들까지 합치면 거진 삼십여 명이었지.”
250|
251|고개를 끄덕인 노인이 얼큰하게 취한 낯빛으로 말을 이었다.
252|
253|“처음에는 다들 그러려니 했네. 이 영인 땅에 한족이 왔던 적이 한두 번도 아니었고, 규모도 그리 크지 않았으니까.”
254|
255|하지만 그건 오판이었다. 노인은 불그스름하게 달아오른 눈빛으로 그날의 기억을 천천히 회상했다.
256|
257|“누구도 예상치 못했던 일이 벌어졌지. 인근의 마을 사람들이 잔치를 열어 놈들을 대접했는데, 하룻밤 사이 모조리 도륙이 난 거야.”
258|
259|“……!”
260|
261|“우리 마을은 다행히 화를 피했지만, 나중에 확인해 보니 그날 밤에만 자그마치 이백여 명이 죽었더군. 사내는 물론이거니와 여인과 아이. 노인까지. 단 한 사람도 살아남지 못했네. 말할 것도 없이 그 한족 놈들의 소행이었지.”
262|
263|“허.”
264|
265|놀랍고도 처참한 이야기다. 이제야 우리를 향해 쏟아졌던 흉흉한 눈빛들과 분위기를 충분히 이해할 수 있었다.
266|
267|더불어 두 개의 단어가 뇌리를 스쳤다.
268|
269|‘암천(暗天). 그리고 남천마후(南天魔后).’
270|
271|천마표국에 포함되었던 한 여인이 마음에 걸리는 건 결코 과민반응이 아니다.
272|
273|심각한 표정으로 이야기를 듣고 있던 화룡각 대원들과 눈빛을 주고받은 나는 인벤토리에 넣어 두었던 종이 한 장을 꺼내 들었다.
274|
275|“말씀 중에 죄송한데, 이것 좀 봐 주시겠습니까?”
276|
277|“이게 뭔가?”
278|
279|내가 꺼낸 종이는 그림이었다.
280|
281|보다 정확히 말하자면 나를 포함한 여러 사람의 증언과 기억을 토대로 만들어진 홍란, 아니 남천마후의 용모파기다.
282|
283|혹시나 하는 마음에 보여 준 것인데, 그림을 확인한 노인의 반응은 미적지근했다.
284|
285|“화공의 솜씨가 대단하군. 한데 이 여인은 누구지?”
286|
287|“음, 아닙니다. 혹시 알고 계신 얼굴인가 해서요.”
288|
289|“그림 속 여인은 본 적 없네. 이토록 아름답다면 어떻게든 기억에 남아 있었겠지. 나 역시 아무리 늙었어도 사내니까.”
290|
291|기대했던 반응은 아니었지만, 크게 실망하는 마음이 들지는 않았다.
292|

*I wondered why we hadn’t met any bandits on the road. Turns out they were in the inn, not the mountains.*

[P87]
It was highway robbery, but now wasn’t the time to save money. I took ten silver nyang from the hefty expense pouch the Murim Alliance had given me and handed them over.

[P88]
“Here. Ten silver nyang.”

[P89]
“For a Han, you catch on quickly.”

[P90]
*Clink.*

[P91]
The old man swept up the gleaming silver with a grin. “Now, what about liquor?”

[P92]
“No, thank you.”

[P93]
“Drink.”

[P94]
“…”

[P95]
“I said drink.”

[P96]
I didn’t have the energy to argue. Looking glum, I opened my pouch again.

[P97]
* * *

[P98]
Our first meal in Nanman was remarkable for all the wrong reasons.

[P99]
The chicken was so scrawny it looked malnourished. The strong liquor had clearly been opened and partly drunk by someone else.

[P100]
It was astonishing that the old man charged us dozens of silver nyang for all this. More astonishing still was how much of the food and liquor he consumed himself.

[P101]
“Burp. That was good.”

[P102]
“…”

[P103]
*Why are you the one who had a good meal?*

[P104]
The question rose to my throat, but I swallowed it. We had bought information with our money and our meal.

[P105]
“The Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau?”

[P106]
“That’s right. I remember them saying they came from Sichuan. One woman and the rest men—nearly thirty people in all.”

[P107]
The old man nodded, his face flushed with drink. “At first, nobody thought much of it. Han Chinese had come to Yeongin before, and their group wasn’t particularly large.”

[P108]
But they had been wrong. His eyes reddened by drink, the old man slowly recalled what had happened.

[P109]
“People from a nearby village held a feast to welcome them. By the next morning, every last one of the villagers had been slaughtered.”

[P110]
“…!”

[P111]
“Our village was spared, thank goodness. But when we checked later, we found that some two hundred people had died that night. Men, women, children, even the elderly. Not one survived. It was those Han bastards’ doing, of course.”

[P112]
“God…”

[P113]
Now I understood the hostile looks we’d drawn on the way here.

[P114]
Two names came to mind.

[P115]
*Dark Heaven. And the Southern Heaven Demon Empress.*

[P116]
That there had been a woman with the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau was more than enough reason to be suspicious.

[P117]
I exchanged glances with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had been listening with grim expressions, then took a sheet of paper from my Inventory.

[P118]
“Sorry to interrupt, but could you look at this?”

[P119]
“What is it?”

[P120]
The paper bore a drawing—or, more precisely, a likeness of Honglan, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, made from several people’s memories and descriptions, including mine.

[P121]
I showed it to him on the off chance he’d recognize her. His reaction was lukewarm.

[P122]
“That artist is quite skilled. Who is she?”

[P123]
“No one. I just wondered if you’d seen her.”

[P124]
“Never seen the woman in that drawing. I’d remember a beauty like that. Old as I am, I’m still a man.”

[P125]
It wasn’t the answer I’d hoped for, but I wasn’t too disappointed. Whatever sort of person the Southern Heaven Demon Empress was, she had a striking appearance. Ju Hwaran had hidden her face with the human-skin mask Song Ilseom made for her. The Demon Empress could have done the same in any number of ways.

[P126]
*It wouldn’t surprise me if she knew an extraordinary disguise technique.*

[P127]
I turned back to the old man. “Where are those Central Plains people from the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau now?”

[P128]
The Quest required us to meet an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, but if those people were still nearby, that changed things.

[P129]
As if reading my thoughts, the old man asked, “Why? Thinking of going after them?”

[P130]
“If we can.”

[P131]
“Admirable, but I doubt you can. It’s been more than half a month.”

[P132]
“If you know which way they went, or have some idea where they were headed, it’s worth a try.”

[P133]
Every Fire Dragon Pavilion member here was formidable. Even Hyuk Mujin, the least skilled among us, was a Supreme First Rate master who had survived countless battles and brushes with death.

[P134]
The old man only gave a short laugh.

[P135]
“It’s impossible.”

[P136]
“Sir, I don’t think you understand—”

[P137]
“I’m not the one who doesn’t understand. Every one of those Central Plains people is dead.”

[P138]
I froze. “What?”

[P139]
“Just what I said. Plenty of tribal warriors were among those killed. Did you think their people would let that go? The Central Plains people died too. We found their bodies not far away. They’d been poisoned with a deadly toxin and collapsed before they could get far.”

[P140]
“…!”

[P141]
“No matter how skilled you are, you can’t chase them into the afterlife. And that goes for…”

[P142]
His voice trailed off. A moment later, he sighed.

[P143]
“…an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion who’s already old as dirt.”

[P144]
*Gulp. Gulp.*

[P145]
The old man drained the last of the strong liquor and smiled at me.

[P146]
“Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”

[P147]
[^1]: Yongsan is a Seoul district where decades of development drove real-estate values sharply upward.
```

## Adjudicator rules

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

*Bang!*

[P24]
Once the door slammed shut behind them, Ju Hwaran spoke with a troubled expression. “Something must have gone badly wrong. It wasn’t like this the last time I came.”

[P25]
Song Ilseom nodded. “I agree. The ethnic groups of Nanman are wary of outsiders, but Yeongin was different. It’s the place closest to the Central Plains.”

[P26]
“Exactly. Merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains used to pass through here. It wasn’t common, but it happened. So why…”

[P27]
As Hwaran trailed off, an elderly voice cut in.

[P28]
“Why? Because of an Escort Bureau. Han bastards just like you.”

[P29]
We weren’t the only ones left in the Poison Flower Pavilion.

[P30]
An old man who had been sleeping off his liquor until a moment ago thumped his bent back and went on. “Bad luck all around. For you lot, crawling into Nanman without knowing what’s happened. And for a certain old man whose business is about to dry up because of those fearless Han bastards.”

[P31]
I realized who he was. “Are you the owner?”

[P32]
The old man looked at me in surprise when I spoke the local language fluently.

[P33]
“You speak our language? Are you Miao?”

[P34]
“No.”

[P35]
“You don’t look Bai or Man, either. With that face, you must be Han Chinese… but you speak it remarkably well. I’d believe you were born and raised here.”

[P36]
As expected of the *Integrated Language Pack*. It certainly did its job.

[P37]
Even Ju Hwaran looked surprised by my pronunciation. “When did you learn their language?”

[P38]
“Well…”

[P39]
I couldn’t exactly explain it, so I let the answer trail off before saying casually, “I picked it up somewhere along the way. Just a little trick.”

[P40]
Beside me, Hyuk Mujin muttered under his breath, “I thought drinking, women, and gambling were the only tricks our Captain knew…”

[P41]
“You little shit.”

[P42]
*Bam!*

[P43]
“Urgh!”

[P44]
Mujin collapsed clutching his solar plexus. The old man clicked his tongue.

[P45]
“That one sure knows how to get himself hit.”

[P46]
“He’s always like that, so don’t mind him… Wait. You speak Chinese?”

[P47]
“To a degree. I served as an interpreter for Han Chinese several times when I was young.”

[P48]
As though it were nothing, the old man pointed a bony finger at Song Ilseom.

[P49]
“That dark-looking fellow seems familiar. Were you here about three years ago?”

[P50]
Ju Hwaran should have stood out most, but perhaps her human-skin mask was why he recognized Song Ilseom first.

[P51]
Song Ilseom nodded silently. The old man slapped his knee.

[P52]
“I knew it. Your name was something like Dragon King…”

[P53]
“Yongbong Escort Bureau. Not Dragon King.”

[P54]
“Right, Yongbong Escort Bureau. Unlike the other merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains, you Han Chinese came by two or three times a year. I remember you clearly.”

[P55]
*For someone who remembers so clearly, you got the name wrong.*

[P56]
I held my tongue and asked what I’d been wanting to ask since he spoke up. “What did you mean earlier?”

[P57]
“Hmm? By what?”

[P58]
“You said an Escort Bureau was why things had gotten like this. In your words, Han bastards like us.”

[P59]
The old man gave me a blank look. “I said that? When?”

[P60]
“What? You definitely—”

[P61]
“Don’t remember a thing.”

[P62]
*Like hell you don’t.*

[P63]
I caught on and sighed. “Food. Can you make us something now?”

[P64]
“Of course. Pay me, and I’ll make you anything.”

[P65]
At the word *food*, Taishan sprang up from where he’d been lying facedown on the table, looking close to death.

[P66]
“Taishan wants five-spice pork!”

[P67]
“So there’s one fellow with more energy than he knows what to do with. I’ll make chicken.”

[P68]
“Why chicken? Taishan doesn’t want chicken! Five-spice pork!”

[P69]
I had no idea how his request for five-spice pork had turned into chicken, but we needed to keep the old man happy. I called to the one person who could stop Taishan’s fit.

[P70]
“Ma Pyo. What are you doing?”

[P71]
“It’s Sama Pyo.”

[P72]
“Right, Sa-pyo.”

[P73]
“…Taishan. Enough. Sit down.”

[P74]
Sama Pyo glared at me before settling Taishan down. Meanwhile, the old man held out his hand as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

[P75]
“What?”

[P76]
“Payment up front.”

[P77]
“Ah.”

[P78]
“Let’s see. One chicken per person is the minimum, so that’s five chickens. At one silver nyang each… ten silver nyang altogether.”

[P79]
“…Ten? At one nyang each, five chickens would cost five.”

[P80]
“Is that so? Then make it two nyang each.”

[P81]
“What?”

[P82]
“I said two nyang per chicken.”

[P83]
“…”

[P84]
“If you don’t like it, spit on the floor and leave. There isn’t another village within a hundred li, mind you.”

[P85]
What a shameless racket. If this man had been born in Yongsan[^1] fifty years ago, he’d have ended up a landlord.

[P86]
*I wondered why we hadn’t met any bandits on the road. Turns out they were in the inn, not the mountains.*

[P87]
It was highway robbery, but now wasn’t the time to save money. I took ten silver nyang from the hefty expense pouch the Murim Alliance had given me and handed them over.

[P88]
“Here. Ten silver nyang.”

[P89]
“For a Han, you catch on quickly.”

[P90]
*Clink.*

[P91]
The old man swept up the gleaming silver with a grin. “Now, what about liquor?”

[P92]
“No, thank you.”

[P93]
“Drink.”

[P94]
“…”

[P95]
“I said drink.”

[P96]
I didn’t have the energy to argue. Looking glum, I opened my pouch again.

[P97]
* * *

[P98]
Our first meal in Nanman was remarkable for all the wrong reasons.

[P99]
The chicken was so scrawny it looked malnourished. The strong liquor had clearly been opened and partly drunk by someone else.

[P100]
It was astonishing that the old man charged us dozens of silver nyang for all this. More astonishing still was how much of the food and liquor he consumed himself.

[P101]
“Burp. That was good.”

[P102]
“…”

[P103]
*Why are you the one who had a good meal?*

[P104]
The question rose to my throat, but I swallowed it. We had bought information with our money and our meal.

[P105]
“The Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau?”

[P106]
“That’s right. I remember them saying they came from Sichuan. One woman and the rest men—nearly thirty people in all.”

[P107]
The old man nodded, his face flushed with drink. “At first, nobody thought much of it. Han Chinese had come to Yeongin before, and their group wasn’t particularly large.”

[P108]
But they had been wrong. His eyes reddened by drink, the old man slowly recalled what had happened.

[P109]
“People from a nearby village held a feast to welcome them. By the next morning, every last one of the villagers had been slaughtered.”

[P110]
“…!”

[P111]
“Our village was spared, thank goodness. But when we checked later, we found that some two hundred people had died that night. Men, women, children, even the elderly. Not one survived. It was those Han bastards’ doing, of course.”

[P112]
“God…”

[P113]
Now I understood the hostile looks we’d drawn on the way here.

[P114]
Two names came to mind.

[P115]
*Dark Heaven. And the Southern Heaven Demon Empress.*

[P116]
That there had been a woman with the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau was more than enough reason to be suspicious.

[P117]
I exchanged glances with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had been listening with grim expressions, then took a sheet of paper from my Inventory.

[P118]
“Sorry to interrupt, but could you look at this?”

[P119]
“What is it?”

[P120]
The paper bore a drawing—or, more precisely, a likeness of Honglan, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, made from several people’s memories and descriptions, including mine.

[P121]
I showed it to him on the off chance he’d recognize her. His reaction was lukewarm.

[P122]
“That artist is quite skilled. Who is she?”

[P123]
“No one. I just wondered if you’d seen her.”

[P124]
“Never seen the woman in that drawing. I’d remember a beauty like that. Old as I am, I’m still a man.”

[P125]
It wasn’t the answer I’d hoped for, but I wasn’t too disappointed. Whatever sort of person the Southern Heaven Demon Empress was, she had a striking appearance. Ju Hwaran had hidden her face with the human-skin mask Song Ilseom made for her. The Demon Empress could have done the same in any number of ways.

[P126]
*It wouldn’t surprise me if she knew an extraordinary disguise technique.*

[P127]
I turned back to the old man. “Where are those Central Plains people from the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau now?”

[P128]
The Quest required us to meet an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, but if those people were still nearby, that changed things.

[P129]
As if reading my thoughts, the old man asked, “Why? Thinking of going after them?”

[P130]
“If we can.”

[P131]
“Admirable, but I doubt you can. It’s been more than half a month.”

[P132]
“If you know which way they went, or have some idea where they were headed, it’s worth a try.”

[P133]
Every Fire Dragon Pavilion member here was formidable. Even Hyuk Mujin, the least skilled among us, was a Supreme First Rate master who had survived countless battles and brushes with death.

[P134]
The old man only gave a short laugh.

[P135]
“It’s impossible.”

[P136]
“Sir, I don’t think you understand—”

[P137]
“I’m not the one who doesn’t understand. Every one of those Central Plains people is dead.”

[P138]
I froze. “What?”

[P139]
“Just what I said. Plenty of tribal warriors were among those killed. Did you think their people would let that go? The Central Plains people died too. We found their bodies not far away. They’d been poisoned with a deadly toxin and collapsed before they could get far.”

[P140]
“…!”

[P141]
“No matter how skilled you are, you can’t chase them into the afterlife. And that goes for…”

[P142]
His voice trailed off. A moment later, he sighed.

[P143]
“…an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion who’s already old as dirt.”

[P144]
*Gulp. Gulp.*

[P145]
The old man drained the last of the strong liquor and smiled at me.

[P146]
“Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”

[P147]
[^1]: Yongsan is a Seoul district where decades of development drove real-estate values sharply upward.
```

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;

Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

For once, he was absolutely right. We couldn’t make enemies of every local in Nanman the moment we arrived.

[P12]
I glanced at the crowd radiating a menacing aura, then opened the door to the Poison Flower Pavilion.

[P13]
*Creeeak.*

[P14]
The old wooden door gave a feeble scrape.

[P15]
Dim light and a gloomy air filled the inn. A few crude tables stood far apart, like weeds growing here and there. The patrons seated at them turned toward us.

[P16]
“Never seen those faces before… Han Chinese?”

[P17]
*Hk, ptui.*

[P18]
Were they Hydras?

[P19]
People around here used phlegm like a passive Skill.

[P20]
The locals spat onto the dusty floor and rose from their seats, their faces flushed from drink.

[P21]
“Han bastards dare come here? Do they want to die?”

[P22]
“They’ve ruined the taste of my liquor. Let’s go. Nothing good will come of staying here with them.”

[P23]
*Bang!*

[P24]
Once the door slammed shut behind them, Ju Hwaran spoke with a troubled expression. “Something must have gone badly wrong. It wasn’t like this the last time I came.”

[P25]
Song Ilseom nodded. “I agree. The ethnic groups of Nanman are wary of outsiders, but Yeongin was different. It’s the place closest to the Central Plains.”

[P26]
“Exactly. Merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains used to pass through here. It wasn’t common, but it happened. So why…”

[P27]
As Hwaran trailed off, an elderly voice cut in.

[P28]
“Why? Because of an Escort Bureau. Han bastards just like you.”

[P29]
We weren’t the only ones left in the Poison Flower Pavilion.

[P30]
An old man who had been sleeping off his liquor until a moment ago thumped his bent back and went on. “Bad luck all around. For you lot, crawling into Nanman without knowing what’s happened. And for a certain old man whose business is about to dry up because of those fearless Han bastards.”

[P31]
I realized who he was. “Are you the owner?”

[P32]
The old man looked at me in surprise when I spoke the local language fluently.

[P33]
“You speak our language? Are you Miao?”

[P34]
“No.”

[P35]
“You don’t look Bai or Man, either. With that face, you must be Han Chinese… but you speak it remarkably well. I’d believe you were born and raised here.”

[P36]
As expected of the *Integrated Language Pack*. It certainly did its job.

[P37]
Even Ju Hwaran looked surprised by my pronunciation. “When did you learn their language?”

[P38]
“Well…”

[P39]
I couldn’t exactly explain it, so I let the answer trail off before saying casually, “I picked it up somewhere along the way. Just a little trick.”

[P40]
Beside me, Hyuk Mujin muttered under his breath, “I thought drinking, women, and gambling were the only tricks our Captain knew…”

[P41]
“You little shit.”

[P42]
*Bam!*

[P43]
“Urgh!”

[P44]
Mujin collapsed clutching his solar plexus. The old man clicked his tongue.

[P45]
“That one sure knows how to get himself hit.”

[P46]
“He’s always like that, so don’t mind him… Wait. You speak Chinese?”

[P47]
“To a degree. I served as an interpreter for Han Chinese several times when I was young.”

[P48]
As though it were nothing, the old man pointed a bony finger at Song Ilseom.

[P49]
“That dark-looking fellow seems familiar. Were you here about three years ago?”

[P50]
Ju Hwaran should have stood out most, but perhaps her human-skin mask was why he recognized Song Ilseom first.

[P51]
Song Ilseom nodded silently. The old man slapped his knee.

[P52]
“I knew it. Your name was something like Dragon King…”

[P53]
“Yongbong Escort Bureau. Not Dragon King.”

[P54]
“Right, Yongbong Escort Bureau. Unlike the other merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains, you Han Chinese came by two or three times a year. I remember you clearly.”

[P55]
*For someone who remembers so clearly, you got the name wrong.*

[P56]
I held my tongue and asked what I’d been wanting to ask since he spoke up. “What did you mean earlier?”

[P57]
“Hmm? By what?”

[P58]
“You said an Escort Bureau was why things had gotten like this. In your words, Han bastards like us.”

[P59]
The old man gave me a blank look. “I said that? When?”

[P60]
“What? You definitely—”

[P61]
“Don’t remember a thing.”

[P62]
*Like hell you don’t.*

[P63]
I caught on and sighed. “Food. Can you make us something now?”

[P64]
“Of course. Pay me, and I’ll make you anything.”

[P65]
At the word *food*, Taishan sprang up from where he’d been lying facedown on the table, looking close to death.

[P66]
“Taishan wants five-spice pork!”

[P67]
“So there’s one fellow with more energy than he knows what to do with. I’ll make chicken.”

[P68]
“Why chicken? Taishan doesn’t want chicken! Five-spice pork!”

[P69]
I had no idea how his request for five-spice pork had turned into chicken, but we needed to keep the old man happy. I called to the one person who could stop Taishan’s fit.

[P70]
“Ma Pyo. What are you doing?”

[P71]
“It’s Sama Pyo.”

[P72]
“Right, Sa-pyo.”

[P73]
“…Taishan. Enough. Sit down.”

[P74]
Sama Pyo glared at me before settling Taishan down. Meanwhile, the old man held out his hand as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

[P75]
“What?”

[P76]
“Payment up front.”

[P77]
“Ah.”

[P78]
“Let’s see. One chicken per person is the minimum, so that’s five chickens. At one silver nyang each… ten silver nyang altogether.”

[P79]
“…Ten? At one nyang each, five chickens would cost five.”

[P80]
“Is that so? Then make it two nyang each.”

[P81]
“What?”

[P82]
“I said two nyang per chicken.”

[P83]
“…”

[P84]
“If you don’t like it, spit on the floor and leave. There isn’t another village within a hundred li, mind you.”

[P85]
What a shameless racket. If this man had been born in Yongsan[^1] fifty years ago, he’d have ended up a landlord.

[P86]
*I wondered why we hadn’t met any bandits on the road. Turns out they were in the inn, not the mountains.*

[P87]
It was highway robbery, but now wasn’t the time to save money. I took ten silver nyang from the hefty expense pouch the Murim Alliance had given me and handed them over.

[P88]
“Here. Ten silver nyang.”

[P89]
“For a Han, you catch on quickly.”

[P90]
*Clink.*

[P91]
The old man swept up the gleaming silver with a grin. “Now, what about liquor?”

[P92]
“No, thank you.”

[P93]
“Drink.”

[P94]
“…”

[P95]
“I said drink.”

[P96]
I didn’t have the energy to argue. Looking glum, I opened my pouch again.

[P97]
* * *

[P98]
Our first meal in Nanman was remarkable for all the wrong reasons.

[P99]
The chicken was so scrawny it looked malnourished. The strong liquor had clearly been opened and partly drunk by someone else.

[P100]
It was astonishing that the old man charged us dozens of silver nyang for all this. More astonishing still was how much of the food and liquor he consumed himself.

[P101]
“Burp. That was good.”

[P102]
“…”

[P103]
*Why are you the one who had a good meal?*

[P104]
The question rose to my throat, but I swallowed it. We had bought information with our money and our meal.

[P105]
“The Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau?”

[P106]
“That’s right. I remember them saying they came from Sichuan. One woman and the rest men—nearly thirty people in all.”

[P107]
The old man nodded, his face flushed with drink. “At first, nobody thought much of it. Han Chinese had come to Yeongin before, and their group wasn’t particularly large.”

[P108]
But they had been wrong. His eyes reddened by drink, the old man slowly recalled what had happened.

[P109]
“People from a nearby village held a feast to welcome them. By the next morning, every last one of the villagers had been slaughtered.”

[P110]
“…!”

[P111]
“Our village was spared, thank goodness. But when we checked later, we found that some two hundred people had died that night. Men, women, children, even the elderly. Not one survived. It was those Han bastards’ doing, of course.”

[P112]
“God…”

[P113]
Now I understood the hostile looks we’d drawn on the way here.

[P114]
Two names came to mind.

[P115]
*Dark Heaven. And the Southern Heaven Demon Empress.*

[P116]
That there had been a woman with the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau was more than enough reason to be suspicious.

[P117]
I exchanged glances with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had been listening with grim expressions, then took a sheet of paper from my Inventory.

[P118]
“Sorry to interrupt, but could you look at this?”

[P119]
“What is it?”

[P120]
The paper bore a drawing—or, more precisely, a likeness of Honglan, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, made from several people’s memories and descriptions, including mine.

[P121]
I showed it to him on the off chance he’d recognize her. His reaction was lukewarm.

[P122]
“That artist is quite skilled. Who is she?”

[P123]
“No one. I just wondered if you’d seen her.”

[P124]
“Never seen the woman in that drawing. I’d remember a beauty like that. Old as I am, I’m still a man.”

[P125]
It wasn’t the answer I’d hoped for, but I wasn’t too disappointed. Whatever sort of person the Southern Heaven Demon Empress was, she had a striking appearance. Ju Hwaran had hidden her face with the human-skin mask Song Ilseom made for her. The Demon Empress could have done the same in any number of ways.

[P126]
*It wouldn’t surprise me if she knew an extraordinary disguise technique.*

[P127]
I turned back to the old man. “Where are those Central Plains people from the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau now?”

[P128]
The Quest required us to meet an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, but if those people were still nearby, that changed things.

[P129]
As if reading my thoughts, the old man asked, “Why? Thinking of going after them?”

[P130]
“If we can.”

[P131]
“Admirable, but I doubt you can. It’s been more than half a month.”

[P132]
“If you know which way they went, or have some idea where they were headed, it’s worth a try.”

[P133]
Every Fire Dragon Pavilion member here was formidable. Even Hyuk Mujin, the least skilled among us, was a Supreme First Rate master who had survived countless battles and brushes with death.

[P134]
The old man only gave a short laugh.

[P135]
“It’s impossible.”

[P136]
“Sir, I don’t think you understand—”

[P137]
“I’m not the one who doesn’t understand. Every one of those Central Plains people is dead.”

[P138]
I froze. “What?”

[P139]
“Just what I said. Plenty of tribal warriors were among those killed. Did you think their people would let that go? The Central Plains people died too. We found their bodies not far away. They’d been poisoned with a deadly toxin and collapsed before they could get far.”

[P140]
“…!”

[P141]
“No matter how skilled you are, you can’t chase them into the afterlife. And that goes for…”

[P142]
His voice trailed off. A moment later, he sighed.

[P143]
“…an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion who’s already old as dirt.”

[P144]
*Gulp. Gulp.*

[P145]
The old man drained the last of the strong liquor and smiled at me.

[P146]
“Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”

[P147]
[^1]: Yongsan is a Seoul district where decades of development drove real-estate values sharply upward.
```

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.
